624.title: Why say what you don't do?
624.word: Why say what you don't do?
624.hook: why do you say what you do not do (61:2–3)
624.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite 61:2–3 when speaking about keeping promises and matching speech to action; many Muslims add in sha' Allah, if God wills, when promising something for the future.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kindness to those who don't fight you, and your line was kindness and justice to all. Who received your one kindness? Today, Surah As-Saff, the Ranks. Day six hundred twenty-four.

We'll grab coffee soon. I'll send you that link. Let me look into it. I'll call Mom this weekend. A busy week leaves a little trail of these behind it, said warmly, meant at the time, and then lost. Nobody's lying exactly. The words just float off ahead of the deeds and never get caught up with. Surah sixty-one opens, right after its first verse of praise, with a question aimed straight at that gap, and the people it asks first are the believers.

Verses two and three. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not? It is most hateful in the sight of Allah that ye say that which ye do not." In Arabic: lima taquluna ma la taf'alun. Why do you say what you don't do? The sound carries the sting: taquluna, you say; taf'alun, you do. The two verbs end alike, and the verse asks why the deeds don't match the words. Then verse three uses a strong word: kabura maqtan. Maqt is intense dislike, disgust. It's grave in God's sight, the verse says. Commentators record that some believers had said, if only we knew which deeds God loves most, we'd do them. Then, when a hard task was asked, some of them held back. The verse catches them in the space between the boast and the moment. The Qur'an returns to this theme. In Surah Hud, the prophet Shu'ayb tells his people that he doesn't want to go behind their backs and do what he forbids them. He won't ask of them what he won't do himself. In Surah Al-Baqarah, people are asked: do you command others to righteousness and forget yourselves? The point is not to stop speaking about the good. It's to close the gap. One practical reading: promise less, and do what you promise. Words are not small here. The verse calls the gap between word and deed most hateful in God's sight.
screen: `TAQULUNA, TAF'ALUN: SAY, DO.` · `KABURA MAQTAN: GRAVELY HATEFUL.` · `SHU'AYB: I DO WHAT I ASK.` · `PROMISE LESS, DO WHAT YOU PROMISE.`

segments.voice: The practice: do one thing you've said you'd do. Sit, and breathe. Scroll back, in your mind, through the last week or two. Find one thing you said you'd do and haven't: a call, a favor, a returned item, a link. Just one. Picture yourself doing it, today, start to finish. Notice any small embarrassment, and let it go on the out-breath. The deed will close the gap better than the guilt. The bell holds the time.
Why say what you don't do? Surah As-Saff asks believers why their words run ahead of their deeds, and calls the gap grave in God's sight. Today's word.
screen: `WHY SAY WHAT YOU DON'T DO? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: say it, do it. Today, do your one promised thing, and make no new promise you can't keep. Day six hundred twenty-four.

625.title: Helpers of Allah
625.hook: be helpers of Allah, as the disciples of Isa said, we are Allah's helpers (61:14)
625.howItsDone: Muslims volunteer at mosques, charities and community kitchens, and speak of service to people in need as helping God's cause; Isa and his disciples are honored in the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why say what you don't do, and your line was say it, do it. Did your promised thing get done? Today, the last verse of Surah As-Saff. Day six hundred twenty-five.

Somebody stands at the front of a room and asks: who'll help? There's a pause. People look at their shoes, or their phones. Then one hand goes up, then another, and suddenly there's a team. A lot of projects, charity drives and community kitchens start in that pause. The last verse of Surah As-Saff takes us back to one of those moments, long before Medina, and to a teacher the Qur'an calls Isa son of Maryam, the man Christians know as Jesus.

Verse fourteen. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Be Allah's helpers, even as Jesus son of Mary said unto the disciples: Who are my helpers for Allah? They said: We are Allah's helpers." The word for helpers is ansar. It's the same word that later named the people of Medina who took in the Prophet ﷺ and the emigrants, the people we met a week ago in the story of the lamp put out. The word for disciples is hawariyyun. Commentators gave different explanations of it. Some said it came from washing and whitening cloth, because some of them were fullers; others said it pointed to the purity of their hearts, or that it simply meant close supporters. The same scene appears in Surah Al 'Imran: Isa senses denial among his people, asks who will be his helpers toward God, and the disciples answer, we are God's helpers, we believe in God, bear witness that we have surrendered. Christians, too, remember a small band of disciples who left their nets to follow Jesus. What does it mean to help God, who needs nothing? Another verse says: if you help God, he will help you and make your feet firm. Commentators explain helping God as helping his cause: his religion and his messengers. Some widen it to the people his law protects, the poor, the orphan, the wronged. The verse doesn't ask for heroes. It asks for the hand that goes up in the pause.
screen: `ANSAR: HELPERS.` · `HAWARIYYUN: THE DISCIPLES.` · `WHO ARE MY HELPERS FOR GOD?` · `HELP HIS CAUSE, AND HE HELPS YOU.`

segments.voice: The practice: help at a mosque or charity. You can't do it in two minutes, but you can choose it. Sit, and breathe. Think of a place near you that runs on helpers: a mosque, a food bank, a shelter, a school, a neighbor who's struggling. Picture the moment someone asks, who'll help? Picture your hand going up. Choose one concrete offer: an hour, a skill, a donation, a lift. The bell holds the time.
Helpers of Allah. Surah As-Saff asks believers to be God's helpers, as the disciples of Isa son of Maryam said they were. Today's word.
Your line: be a helper. Today, make your offer: send the message, sign up, or put your hand up the next time someone asks. Day six hundred twenty-five.

626.title: Hasten to the remembrance
626.hook: when the call is made on Friday, hasten to remember Allah and leave trade (62:9)
626.howItsDone: On Fridays, many Muslims bathe, wear clean clothes, and go to the mosque for the congregational prayer, which has a sermon and two units of prayer in place of the noon prayer; most jurists hold it obligatory for adult, resident men, and women may attend.

segments.voice: Yesterday, helpers of Allah, and your line was be a helper. Did your hand go up somewhere? Today, Surah Al-Jumu'ah, named for Friday. Day six hundred twenty-six.

Friday, a little after noon, in a busy city. A shopkeeper pulls down the shutter halfway and hangs a sign. A taxi driver parks two streets away. Office workers drift out of glass towers in twos and threes, some still on their phones. A boy is running because he's late. They're all heading the same way, toward the sound of the call. For about an hour, buying and selling stops. Surah sixty-two, Al-Jumu'ah, is where that hour comes from.

Verse nine. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading." The day of congregation is yawm al-jumu'ah, from the root j-m-', to gather. Friday is literally gathering day. The prayer that replaces the noon prayer that day has a sermon, the khutbah, and two units of prayer, prayed together. Now, the verb for hasten is fas'aw. Does that mean run? Commentators said no. Bukhari records that the Prophet ﷺ told people not to rush to the prayer but to walk with calm and dignity, even if they'd miss part of it. So fas'aw means go with intent, set out with purpose, not sprint. And leave your trading is concrete: when the call comes, the deal can wait. Hadith fill in the morning before. Bukhari records that whoever bathes on Friday and goes early to the prayer is like one who offered a camel; a little later, a cow; then a ram, then a hen, then an egg. And when the imam comes out to give the sermon, the angels close their records and sit down to listen. Who is the Friday prayer required of? Most jurists say adult men who are resident and able; women may attend and many do, and for travelers and the sick it's lifted. The verse ends: that is better for you, if you only knew. One hour of the week, cut out of the market, and handed back to remembrance.
screen: `JUMU'AH: GATHERING DAY.` · `FAS'AW: SET OUT WITH PURPOSE.` · `COME EARLY: A CAMEL, THEN AN EGG.` · `THE ANGELS CLOSE THEIR RECORDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: arrive early to something. Sit, and breathe. Think of the next thing you're due at: a prayer, a meeting, a class, a meal with someone. Picture yourself arriving ten minutes early, walking calmly, not rushing. Picture the room before anyone else is there, and you, settled, unhurried, ready to listen. Let your breath slow to that pace now. The bell holds the time.
Hasten to the remembrance. When the call for Friday prayer comes, Surah Al-Jumu'ah says, set out for the remembrance of God and leave your trade. Today's word.
Your line: leave trade for a while. Today, arrive early to one thing, and spend the extra minutes simply waiting, phone away. Day six hundred twenty-six.

627.title: Then go out and seek
627.hook: when the prayer is done, disperse and seek Allah's bounty (62:10)
627.howItsDone: After the Friday prayer, many Muslims return to work or business; Friday is a day of congregation rather than a required day of rest, though some countries include it in the weekend.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hasten to the remembrance, and your line was leave trade for a while. What did you arrive early to, and what did the waiting feel like? Day six hundred twenty-seven.

The Friday prayer ends. People stand, shake hands, find their shoes in the pile by the door. Within ten minutes, the shutters are back up, the taxis are moving, the office towers are filling again. A holy day might sound like a day off, a whole day set apart from work and money. The very next verse of Surah Al-Jumu'ah doesn't tell people to stay. It sends them out the door.
screen: `SHOES FROM THE PILE BY THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Verse ten. Pickthall: "And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty, and remember Allah much, that ye may be successful." Three verbs. Fantashiru, disperse, spread out through the land. Wabtaghu, seek, from God's bounty, fadl, which commentators read here as earning a living. And udhkuru, remember God much. Commentators read the command to go out as a permission, not an obligation: the restriction of the previous verse is lifted. Still, the order is telling. In these verses, Friday isn't a day off. It's a day with one hour carved out for gathering, and then work resumes, with remembrance carried into it. Then verse eleven tells a story against the community itself. While the Prophet ﷺ was giving the sermon one Friday, a trade caravan arrived in Medina. People slipped out to it, and left him standing. Bukhari and Muslim report that only twelve men remained. The verse records it plainly, and adds: what is with God is better than amusement and trade, and God is the best of providers. So verses nine to eleven make a little circle. Leave trade for the prayer. After the prayer, go seek a living. But never leave the prayer for the trade. Remembrance at the center, work around it, and the word much: remember God much, not only in the mosque, but out in the market too.
screen: `DISPERSE, SEEK, REMEMBER.` · `NOT A DAY OFF.` · `THE CARAVAN AND THE TWELVE.` · `REMEMBER GOD MUCH, OUT IN THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: The practice: work well after praying. Sit, and breathe. If you pray, think of your next prayer, and the work that follows it. If you don't, think of this sit as your pause. Now picture the very next task waiting for you. See yourself starting it calmly, carrying a little of this quiet into it, doing it carefully, as if it counted. Choose one way you'll do it a little better than usual. The bell holds the time.
Then go out and seek. When the prayer is done, Surah Al-Jumu'ah says, disperse through the land, seek God's bounty, and remember God much. Today's word.
screen: `THEN GO OUT AND SEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pray, then work. Today, after your pause, do your next task well, and remember once in the middle of it. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

628.title: Fine bodies, empty words
628.hook: their bodies impress you and their speech charms you, but they're like propped-up timber (63:4)
628.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often use the signs of the hypocrite from the hadith as a checklist for self-examination, and the story of Hanzala is told to reassure believers that changing moods are not hypocrisy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, then go out and seek, and your line was pray, then work. Did your next task get done a little better? Today, Surah Al-Munafiqun. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Walk through a film set and you'll see a whole street: shop fronts, balconies, a church tower. Walk around the back and it's plywood and scaffolding, held up by diagonal beams. From the front, perfect. From behind, nothing. Surah sixty-three is about people in Medina who were a little like that street. It's named for them: Al-Munafiqun. And in one verse, it gives them an image so vivid it's hard to forget.

Verse four. Pickthall: "And when thou seest them their figures please thee; and if they speak thou givest ear unto their speech. (They are) as though they were blocks of wood in striped cloaks." The Arabic image is khushubun musannadah: timber propped up against a wall. Wood that looks solid, but can't stand on its own, with nothing living in it. Fine bodies, polished words, and inside, no root. The word for what the surah describes is nifaq. Classical Arabic dictionaries connect it to the nafiqa', a burrow some desert animals dig with a hidden second exit: one way in that everyone sees, and another way out that no one does. Nifaq is having two doors. In the Qur'an, the munafiqun are people who declared faith in Medina while working against the community in secret. But the hadith also turns the word into a mirror for believers. Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ naming the signs: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; when he's trusted, he betrays. And Muslim records a tender scene. Abu Bakr met a companion named Hanzala and asked how he was. Hanzala answered: Hanzala has become a hypocrite! With the Prophet, he said, he felt paradise and hell before his eyes; at home with his wife and children, he forgot. Abu Bakr said, I feel the same. They went to the Prophet, who told them: if you stayed always as you are with me, angels would shake your hands in the street. But Hanzala, an hour and an hour. In this report, the worry about being two-faced is not treated as nifaq. It's answered gently.
screen: `PROPPED-UP TIMBER.` · `NIFAQ: A BURROW WITH TWO DOORS.` · `LIES, BROKEN PROMISES, BETRAYAL.` · `HANZALA: AN HOUR AND AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: The practice: check your words against your deeds. Sit, and breathe. Gently, without harshness, look at one place where your outside and inside don't match: a face you wear in one room and not another. Don't scold yourself. Hanzala's worry was met with gentleness. Just name it, and choose one small way to bring the two sides a little closer. The bell holds the time.
Nifaq. Hypocrisy: a burrow with two doors, a fine front with timber propped up behind it. Today's word.
Your line: not propped up. Today, do one thing that matches what you say you care about, where no one will see it. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

629.title: Don't let them distract you
629.hook: let neither wealth nor children distract you from remembering Allah (63:9)
629.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to pray with presence of heart, and some silence phones and choose a quiet place; 63:9–11 is recited as a reminder to give in charity before death comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nifaq, and your line was not propped up. What did you do where no one could see it? Day six hundred twenty-nine.

A parent stands in prayer. Behind them, a toddler is narrating a cartoon at full volume. The phone on the shelf buzzes: a client, an invoice, the bank. Somewhere in the middle of the second unit, the parent realizes they've been planning dinner. None of these things are bad. The child is loved. The work feeds the child. That's exactly what makes them so good at pulling attention away. Surah Al-Munafiqun, after its warnings, turns to the believers and names those two pulls.

Verse nine. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Let not your wealth nor your children distract you from remembrance of Allah." The verb is tulhikum, from the root l-h-w, the same root as lahw, the amusement we met in Surah Al-Hadid two weeks ago. Distraction and amusement are the same family: whatever fills your attention so completely that something more important slips out. And notice what the verse names. Not sins. Wealth and children, two things the Qur'an elsewhere calls the adornment of worldly life. The danger isn't in them. It's in how easily they can take up the whole field of view. Surah At-Takathur says it in one line: the rivalry for more distracts you, until you visit the graves. Same root, same pull. Then verse ten turns urgent. Spend from what God has provided, before death comes to one of you and he says: my Lord, if only you'd give me a little more time, I would give in charity and be among the righteous. Verse eleven answers: God does not delay a soul when its term has come. So the verse doesn't say: have less, love less. It says: remember through it. The parent doesn't stop being a parent in prayer. The worker doesn't stop working. But somewhere in the noise, there is a thread back to God, and the verse asks believers not to let it drop. Those who do, it says, are the losers.
screen: `TULHIKUM: FROM L-H-W.` · `WEALTH AND CHILDREN, NOT SINS.` · `IF ONLY I HAD A LITTLE MORE TIME.` · `REMEMBER THROUGH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: a phone-free prayer. Put your phone in another room, or face down and silent, out of reach. If you pray, pray your next prayer this way, and notice what pulls at you. If you don't, sit now, without it, for the length of the bell. Each time your mind runs to the screen, the inbox, the next errand, notice the pull, name it gently, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Don't let them distract you. Surah Al-Munafiqun asks believers not to let wealth or children distract them from remembering God. Today's word.
screen: `DON'T LET THEM DISTRACT YOU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: remember through it all. Today, in the busiest moment of your day, find one breath to remember, right there in the noise. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

630.title: He guides the heart
630.hook: no calamity strikes except by Allah's leave, and whoever believes, He guides his heart (64:11)
630.carry: he guides the heart through it
630.howItsDone: When news of a loss comes, Muslims widely say 'inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un', we belong to God and to him we return, and many add the supplication the Prophet taught Umm Salama.

segments.voice: Yesterday, don't let them distract you, and your line was remember through it all. Did you find one breath in the busiest moment? Today, Surah At-Taghabun. Day six hundred thirty, the end of the week.

Medina, a small house. A woman named Umm Salama has just lost her husband, Abu Salama, and the grief is still new. She remembers something the Prophet ﷺ had taught: words to say when a loss strikes. She starts to say them, and then stops, thinking: who could be better than Abu Salama? She says them anyway. Hold that moment. Today's verse is about what happens inside a heart at exactly that point.

Surah At-Taghabun, verse eleven. Pickthall: "No calamity befalleth save by Allah's leave. And whosoever believeth in Allah, He guideth his heart." The word for calamity is musiba, anything that strikes, from a root meaning to hit the mark. The verse makes two claims. First, nothing happens outside God's permission. Second, and this is the tender part: for the one who believes, God guides the heart. Not removes the calamity. Guides the heart through it. A student of the companions named 'Alqama explained the verse simply. It's the person struck by a loss, he said, who knows it is from God, and so accepts it and is content. Guidance here isn't an answer to why. It's a steadiness that comes in the middle of the not-knowing. Back to Umm Salama. Muslim records the words the Prophet had taught: we belong to God and to him we return; O God, reward me in my calamity and give me something better in its place. The first half is from the Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah. Pickthall: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Umm Salama said it, doubting. Later, the Prophet himself asked to marry her, and she became one of the mothers of the believers. She'd say afterward that God had given her better than Abu Salama: the Messenger of God. The verse doesn't promise the story always turns out like hers. It promises something smaller and closer: a guided heart, steadied in the loss, before anything else changes.

segments.voice: The practice: accept one setback calmly. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one recent setback, not the biggest grief, something smaller: a plan that fell through, a no, a loss of time or money. Let yourself feel it honestly. Then, if you pray, say the words Umm Salama said: we belong to God, and to him we return. If not, simply breathe out slowly and let your shoulders drop, accepting that it happened. The bell holds the time.
He guides the heart. No calamity strikes except by God's leave, and whoever believes in God, he guides that person's heart. Today's word.

Your line: he guides the heart through it. This week ran from say it, do it, through God's helpers and the Friday prayer, to propped-up timber, distraction and Umm Salama's words. Today, meet one setback calmly. Day six hundred thirty.
